column4: The man could have been raised through the signs, but أَخْلَدَ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ, clung to the earth; this states the section's vertical choice almost exactly.
The summons to go forth meets people who ٱثَّاقَلْتُمْ إِلَى ٱلْأَرْضِ, grow heavy toward the earth, making attachment to the nearer life bodily immobility.
The only other Qur'anic لِبَدًا pictures people nearly becoming a compact mass upon God's servant, preserving the source word's piled, inseparable layers in a crowd.
A showy spender is bare rock thinly covered by تُرَابٌ until a downpour strips it; rain, soil, and false expenditure expose how little the apparent heap holds.
These poor are restrained in God's way and لَا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ ضَرْبًا فِي الْأَرْضِ; their inability to travel concretizes both the stationary miskīn and the dictionary's non-travelling lubad.
At judgment the denier wishes, يَٰلَيْتَنِى كُنتُ تُرَابًا; the earth beneath the destitute becomes the wished-for refuge of one whose deeds and possessions cannot save him.
Face-down movement is set against upright walking on a straight path, turning the section's horizontal body and rising road into an explicit test of guidance.
حُبًّا جَمًّا describes massed, consuming love of wealth; the source itself identifies جَمًّا as the Qur'anic gloss of the piled لُبَدًا.
Poor believers want to travel but turn back weeping because no mount can be found; want of property literally fixes them in place.
The blame falls on affluent men who ask to remain with those left behind; beside 9:92, abundance and lack produce the two forms of earthbound stillness developed in the section.
The owner of immense treasure is swallowed together with his house by the earth, making amassed wealth and downward attachment one literal scene.
وَمَا يُغْنِى عَنْهُ مَالُهُ إِذَا تَرَدَّىٰ asks what wealth can do when its owner falls headlong; the heap cannot arrest the downward movement it encouraged.
Rivalry in accumulation distracts people; read with 102:2, the activity that builds the heap runs only until its owners reach the graves.
حَتَّىٰ زُرْتُمُ الْمَقَابِرَ completes 102:1 by placing accumulators in the cemetery, the terminal soil sense that the section finds inside balad and turbah.
The person who جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ turns wealth into a counted mass, a direct behavioral form of مَالًا لُبَدًا.
A rich garden-owner who boasts of wealth is reminded that his Creator made him مِن تُرَابٍ; the rebuke puts the affluent man on the same dust as the destitute.
A raven works the earth to teach burial of a corpse; bird, ground, and grave meet the dictionary's crouching bird and turbah of the dead in one scene.
The sacrificial animals stand, then their sides fall to earth and their flesh feeds the content and the beggar; bodily descent becomes provision for someone in need.
Pack animals carry burdens to a بَلَدٍ reachable only with bodily hardship, joining the city, travel, weight, and the labor required to overcome staying in place.
Measured rain is made to settle in the earth, فَأَسْكَنَّاهُ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ; the س ك ن root here gives life by coming to rest rather than naming deprivation's arrested motion.
Abraham says أَسْكَنتُ of settling his family in an uncultivated valley, then asks for provision; settlement, barren ground, mobility, and sustenance converge.
Homes are made سَكَنًا while hide tents are light on travel and encampment days; the ayah itself distinguishes chosen repose from the inability to depart.
A settled town receives provision abundantly from every direction, then is clothed in hunger after ingratitude; plenty and destitution occupy the same place in succession.
Saba's dwelling is a sign with two gardens and the words بَلْدَةٌ طَيِّبَةٌ; balad here is an inhabited, provision-bearing ground rather than grave-soil.
People are called to spend but withhold, although وَٱللَّهُ ٱلْغَنِىُّ وَأَنتُمُ ٱلْفُقَرَاءُ; this overturns the rich person's imagined height and locates need universally.
Distribution to orphans, the needy, and travelers is ordered so wealth does not merely circulate among the rich; the rule directly prevents wealth from matting into one social layer.
Hoarded gold and silver are paired with refusal to spend in God's way, defining the moral danger of wealth kept compact instead of released toward need.
The hoard of 9:34 is heated and pressed onto foreheads, sides, and backs; stored wealth becomes a material weight upon the body that amassed it.
What the affluent withhold will be made a collar around them at resurrection; retained bounty becomes the fastening that holds its possessor.
جَمَعَ فَأَوْعَىٰ presents the person who collects and seals wealth away, a concise parallel to possessions compacted into an unmoving heap.
The garden owners command that no miskīn enter that day; accumulated produce is guarded by excluding the very earthbound poor person the section commands one to approach.
After barring the miskīn in 68:24, the owners say بَلْ نَحْنُ مَحْرُومُونَ; those with abundance become the deprived, reversing the two positions.
Failure to urge feeding the miskīn immediately precedes devouring inheritance and loving amassed wealth, supplying the neglected person on the other side of 89:20's heap.
Inheritance is devoured with all-consuming greed between neglect of the poor and love of massed wealth, showing how the heap is produced by taking rather than bending down to give.
The prayerful have a known right within their wealth; the heap is opened by recognizing that part of it already belongs beyond its possessor.
The fixed share of 70:24 belongs to the asker and the deprived, placing the needy person structurally inside, rather than outside, accumulated property.
In their wealth is a right for the asker and the deprived; this directly joins held property to the person scarcity has brought low.
They feed the miskīn, orphan, and captive despite loving the food, enacting the section's claim that ascent requires turning beloved provision toward the lowly.
Righteousness includes giving wealth despite love of it to the needy and traveler and freeing people; it turns possessed wealth into the very acts defining the steep ascent in surah 90.
The miser who considers himself self-sufficient, ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ, embodies the dictionary's opposite pole of dust: imagined richness that leaves its owner unwilling to give.
Intense love of wealth supplies the attachment whose earthly endpoint appears immediately in the opened graves of 100:9.
When what lies in the graves is scattered out, the intense wealth-love of 100:8 reaches the soil and burial horizon developed in the section.
The garden-owner boasts that he is greater in wealth and stronger in followers, a narrative counterpart to the boast over piled wealth in 90:6.
The boaster's produce is destroyed and he turns his hands over what he spent while the garden lies collapsed, bringing vaunted property physically down.
Qarun's treasure keys burden a strong company; abundance is represented as compact, bodily weight before the earth swallows it in 28:81.
Qarun is told to seek the final abode through what God gave him and to do good; wealth could raise its holder only by being redirected from self-attachment.
Those who wished for Qarun's station recognize that provision is expanded or restricted and that they too could have been swallowed, undoing the equation of abundance with height.
Even مِلْءُ ٱلْأَرْضِ ذَهَبًا cannot ransom the one who dies rejecting faith; wealth literally measured by an earthful ends powerless before death.
Those staying behind rejoice in sitting and dislike striving with wealth and lives; possession and attachment produce the dictionary's person who will not travel.
Men of means request exemption so they can be among the sitters, again making abundance rather than incapacity the cause of immobility.
Sedentary believers, apart from the disabled, are distinguished from those who strive with wealth and lives; property may either anchor its holder or become the means of movement.
Those who remained behind say أَمْوَٰلُنَا وَأَهْلُونَا شَغَلَتْنَا; wealth itself is offered as what kept its owners from setting out.
No expenditure small or great and no valley crossed goes unrecorded; the ayah unites the source expression's little-or-much wealth with actual departure and passage.
Earth is made tractable: people are told to walk its slopes and eat God's provision; ground becomes a traversable source of sustenance rather than a surface that pins one down.
The winter and summer journeys define movement away from and back to the settled sacred place; 106:4 states that these journeys culminate in food and security.
The Lord of the House feeds Quraysh against hunger and secures them against fear, placing provision within the same Meccan ground called البلد in surah 90.
Human beings are created from earth, returned into it, and brought out again; soil is origin, grave, and the point from which immobility will be reversed.
God causes humanity to grow from the earth like a growth; 71:18 then returns them into the same ground and brings them forth.
Return into earth is followed by a decisive bringing forth, so grave-soil is a temporary enclosure rather than permanent sticking.
At one call people emerge from the earth; the final divine summons reverses the stillness of burial immediately and bodily.
The earth is made كِفَاتًا, a containing place; 77:26 specifies that its gathered contents are both the living and the dead.
أَحْيَاءً وَأَمْوَاتًا makes one earth hold inhabited life and buried death, joining the settlement and cemetery senses developed for balad.
At the trumpet people rush from graves to their Lord; movement erupts from the place that had held the dead motionless.
When graves are overturned and their contents thrown out, burial ground can no longer keep bodies pressed within it.
This ayah identifies the man as one given God's signs who stripped himself from them; it makes 7:176's earthward clinging a response to revelation, as in surah 90's بِـَٔايَٰتِنَا.
Abraham asks that this become a secure بَلَدًا and that its people receive fruits; inhabited place is expressly joined to safety and provision.
Abraham asks that هَٰذَا ٱلْبَلَدَ be secure, echoing surah 90's demonstrative city while 14:37 supplies settlement in its barren ground and the prayer for fruit.
The oath وَهَٰذَا ٱلْبَلَدِ ٱلْأَمِينِ repeats the deictic city of 90:1 and marks that settled ground by security.
Rain is driven to لِبَلَدٍ مَّيِّتٍ and brings out fruits; balad takes the land/soil sense, while water raises provision from what lay dead.
The good balad brings vegetation by God's leave while the bad yields only scantily, tying the character of ground to abundance and scarcity.
Rain revives بَلْدَةً مَّيْتًا and waters animals and many people; dead ground becomes the means of relieving bodily need.
Clouds are driven to a dead بَلَدٍ and the earth is revived; rain's effect is life and lifting rather than the lexicon's compression of soil.
Measured water revives a dead بَلْدَةً, followed by the comparison to being brought out; the soil sense of balad opens onto resurrection.
Rain is provision for servants and revives a dead بَلْدَةً; emergence from death is compared to produce rising from watered ground.
أَسْكِنُوهُنَّ commands housing vulnerable women where the addressees dwell and according to their means; settled space and material capacity become care rather than exclusion.
People of abundance are forbidden to stop giving to kin, the needy, and emigrants; wealth and social elevation must bend toward those exposed by need and displacement.
The collector imagines his wealth makes him endure; 104:4 immediately answers the fantasy with being cast into the Crusher.
لَيُنبَذَنَّ فِى ٱلْحُطَمَةِ answers the counted heap by throwing its owner downward, turning presumed permanence into violent abasement.
The one who does not urge feeding the miskīn is condemned, the direct negative of stooping toward the ground-bound poor through food.
Failure to urge feeding the miskīn is named among the causes of punishment, making neglect of the lowly a decisive spiritual failure.
The condemned confess that they did not feed the miskīn; their own speech identifies the missed act that the steep ascent requires.
Wealth spent in God's way becomes a grain rising into seven ears and multiplied yield; release upward and outward answers wealth compacted into a sterile heap.
Sincere spenders are a garden on a height whose downpour doubles its fruit, reversing 2:264's rain-stripped dust and the section's rain-beaten ground.
Human origin in تُرَابٍ is joined to lifeless earth that trembles and swells after water; the same ground that receives bodies visibly rises.
Earth seen خَاشِعَةً stirs and swells when water descends, a precise upward reversal of soil flattened and matted by rain.
Water is poured abundantly before 80:26's splitting of earth; rain initiates opening rather than compression.
ثُمَّ شَقَقْنَا ٱلْأَرْضَ شَقًّا makes the watered ground split apart so food can emerge, the opposite physical movement from felting soil into one layer.
Created مِن تُرَابٍ, humans then تَنتَشِرُونَ, spread abroad; dust-origin issues in dispersal and movement rather than adhesion to the ground.
Birds held in the open sky provide the direct vertical opposite of the dictionary's bird crouched and stuck upon earth.
Birds above spread and fold their wings while the Merciful holds them; elevation and divine holding reverse the earth-clinging bird sense of lubad.
Night is given so people may rest, لِتَسْكُنُوا, and day so they may seek bounty; wholesome stillness alternates with provision-seeking movement.
After prayer people are told to disperse through the earth and seek God's bounty, the active opposite of both the non-travelling lubad and poverty-enforced stillness.
Some travel through the earth seeking God's bounty; movement is the means to provision here, clarifying what the immobilized poor of 2:273 cannot do.
All people are ٱلْفُقَرَاءُ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ while God alone is rich, collapsing the earthly distinction between the possessor of the heap and the destitute beside him.
God found the addressee عَائِلًا and made him self-sufficient, showing need and sufficiency as reversible conditions rather than fixed human heights.
The command to descend is followed by an earthly place of settlement and temporary enjoyment; life on the ground is expressly a limited stay.
Living, dying, and being brought out all occur in relation to the earth, completing 7:24's settlement with its grave and exit.
God produced humanity from earth and settled or enabled it to flourish there, making attachment to ground a constructive trust rather than moral collapse.
Saba's turn from gratitude brings a flood and replacement of its abundant gardens with meager growth, reversing 34:15's good, provision-bearing balad.
Heaped quantities of gold and silver are among the beautified desires of near life; the verse names both the mass and the attachment that make wealth earthward.
Worldly rivalry in wealth is compared to rain-grown vegetation that dries and becomes debris, making material accumulation part of an earthly cycle that will not remain.
The one who gives and is mindful begins the opposite course from 92:8's miser; giving is the first movement toward the ease promised in 92:7.
Ease is facilitated for the giver described in 92:5-6, paralleling ascent through releasing wealth toward another.
Difficulty is facilitated for the miser who deems himself self-sufficient, preparing the fall in 92:11.
When good touches the anxious human he becomes withholding; material ease paradoxically arrests outward movement of provision.
The devil threatens poverty when people are called to spend, exposing fear of becoming destitute as a force that keeps wealth compacted.
At judgment the speaker admits that his wealth did not avail him; property that seemed protective has no power at the final descent.
Abu Lahab's wealth and gains do not avail him, another concise boundary on what a possessed heap can secure.
Giving the needy and traveler their due directs property toward both poverty and movement, the two pressures gathered in the stationary miskīn image.
The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor extended without limit; provision is released without turning the giver into someone stripped and grounded by want.
The addressee must remain with humble worshippers and not let his eyes pass beyond them toward worldly adornment, a social form of bending toward the lowly rather than wealth.
The one who considers himself self-sufficient receives attention, while the vulnerable seeker is neglected in the surrounding scene; the stance reverses the section's demanded inclination.
Being distracted from the earnest blind visitor completes the scene begun in 80:1-2 and 80:5, showing what it means to turn away from someone socially brought low.
Helpless men, women, and children cannot devise a plan or find a way, a broader instance of vulnerability expressed as inability to move.
The emigrant who moves through the earth finds many refuges and abundance, giving a mobility-and-provision counter-scene to being fixed by need.
Lowering the wing of humility in mercy toward vulnerable parents gives the section's claim a bodily ethic: moral height appears through deliberate lowering toward another.
The arrogant walker can neither split the earth nor reach the mountains in height; human pretension is bounded between ground and elevation.
The command to go forth light or heavy and strive with wealth and lives directly reverses 9:38's earthward heaviness and shows wealth put into motion.
Following 22:5's dust-origin and rain-raised ground, this ayah states that God will raise those in graves; burial's stillness is explicitly temporary.
Pilgrims eat from sacrificial animals and feed the afflicted poor, so an animal brought down becomes provision for someone brought low by need.
Those claiming helplessness are asked whether God's earth was not spacious enough to migrate; 4:98 then distinguishes people whose immobility is real.
Poor emigrants are expelled from homes and possessions yet move in search of God's bounty, a direct counter-scene to poverty that prevents travel.
People already settled in the abode prefer displaced newcomers over themselves despite their own privation, joining settlement, scarcity, and the outward release of goods.
The Prophet is told not to fix his eyes on others' worldly enjoyment but to lower his wing to believers; material height is exchanged for deliberate social lowering.
Prostrate and draw near makes bodily descent the means of nearness, a compact spiritual parallel to rising by bending toward one already low.
Believers are told to spend from good earnings and from what God brings out of the earth, directly joining ground, provision, and wealth released toward others.
Even everything on earth and its equal cannot ransom a disbeliever from judgment; possessions measured by the whole earth reach an absolute limit.
Wrongdoers would offer all that is on earth and its like as ransom; the imagined earth-sized fortune cannot lift its possessor from judgment.
Those who do not answer God would ransom themselves with all the earth's contents and as much again, another exact earth-measure of futile abundance.
Every wrongdoing soul would offer all that is on earth as ransom when punishment is seen, making earth-filled possession powerless at the final reckoning.
The earth splits from people as they emerge hurriedly; ground releases the buried into swift movement, reversing both grave enclosure and arrested motion.
The earth casts out its burdens, turning what lay pressed and hidden within burial ground outward.
People emerge from graves like scattered locusts, replacing the grave's stillness with dispersal and mass movement.
People rush from graves as though racing toward a marker; the formerly earth-held body becomes urgently mobile.
Wealth and children must not distract from God's remembrance; possession becomes loss when its accumulated claims hold the owner in the nearer life.
People must spend from provision before death and the futile request for delay; the stored heap must be opened before its owner reaches the grave.
If humans possessed the treasuries of divine mercy, they would withhold them from fear of spending, exposing the impulse that compresses abundance into a guarded mass.
A promise to give charity if granted bounty sets the proper outward movement of abundance before 9:76 records its reversal.
When bounty arrives, the recipients become miserly and turn away; increase itself produces closure instead of the promised care for others.
The miserly both withhold God's bounty and instruct others to withhold, allowing accumulated wealth to harden into a social practice.
Those who are miserly and command miserliness are answered by God's self-sufficiency, setting the closed human heap against the only true richness.
The hypocrites propose withholding support until the Prophet's companions disperse; wealth is deliberately used to uproot vulnerable people from their place.
Withholding even ordinary aid completes the passage that refuses food to the miskīn, showing the small, everyday closure behind neglect of the poor.
Giving the needy and traveler their due places property at the service of both destitution and mobility.
The answer about spending directs wealth to parents, kin, orphans, the needy, and the traveler, opening possessions toward people whose support or movement has failed.
Obligatory alms belong to the poor, the needy, and the stranded traveler among others; accumulated property is assigned to both want and interrupted movement.
The speaker is commanded to worship the Lord of this بَلْدَة, who made it sacred; the city is a divinely bounded settled place rather than mere soil.
A secure sanctuary is set amid people being snatched away around it, clarifying the Meccan city's character as stable refuge within dangerous movement.
Worship of the Lord of this House supplies the fixed sacred center between the journeys of 106:2 and the food and security of 106:4.
Birds glorify with wings outspread, another explicit airborne posture opposite the dictionary's bird crouched against earth.
Human transgression begins when a person sees himself as self-sufficient; imagined richness supplies the stance behind boastful possession and refusal to give.
Those who are poor are promised enrichment from God's bounty within a command of communal care, presenting poverty and sufficiency as transformable conditions.
Fear of poverty is answered by God's promise of enrichment from His bounty, so anticipated want need not harden people into withholding.
Wealth and children are the adornment of near life, while enduring good deeds are better in reward and hope; possession is denied lasting vertical worth.
The day when neither wealth nor children benefit sets a direct boundary on what the amassed heap can carry beyond earthly life.
Water from the sky gives life to earth after its death, reversing the lexicon's rain-compressed soil through a life-giving transformation.
Rain sent from the sky revives earth after death; repeated Qur'anic formulation makes water an agent of release and life rather than mere flattening.
Rainwater revives earth after its death, embedding the upward recovery of ground within the signs of lightning, fear, and hope.
The effects of divine mercy are visible in earth revived after death, and that reviver will raise the dead; soil's recovery becomes the model for bodies leaving it.
Provision sent from the sky revives earth after death, joining rain, ground, and sustenance in the opposite movement from pressed barrenness.
God's revival of earth after death supplies a repeated boundary to the grave and motionless-soil senses developed in the section.
Water descends and the earth becomes green; the surface responds to rain with visible life rather than remaining a compacted layer.
Those in graves cannot be made to hear; the grave is pictured through the stillness and unresponsiveness that the section associates with lost movement.
The unwilling would travel for nearby gain and an easy journey but find the distance too great, showing material advantage governing whether bodies leave the ground.
The weak, ill, and those lacking anything to spend are excused from going forth, distinguishing need-enforced stillness before the weeping would-be travelers of 9:92.
The Children of Israel are told to dwell in the land, then are gathered at the final promise; settled residence eventually yields to divinely compelled movement.
Lowering one's wing to believing followers repeats the bodily ethic of descending toward people under one's care.
The Prophet must not drive away humble worshippers seeking their Lord; nearness to the socially lowly outweighs elite pressure and status.
Night is made سَكَنًا, a beneficial cessation of motion; this natural repose clarifies by contrast the deprivation encoded in miskīn's enforced stillness.
Night is made for rest and day for sight, placing stillness inside a sustaining rhythm rather than making it the permanent condition of poverty.
Night in which people rest is a divine sign, another positive use of the س ك ن root against involuntary social immobility.
Night is made for rest and day for sight through divine bounty, connecting repose to provision while distinguishing it from need that arrests movement.
